We present SentryBench, which scores agents on a two-sided, cost-sensitive frontier jointly measuring attack success, over-refusal (missing a real emergency), and over-reaction (unwarranted action) under adversarial tool use, with scenarios grounded in real emergency-call transcripts, disaster messages, and real injection/jailbreak payloads. We formalize deployment harm as an asymmetric cost functional, prove naive caution is harm-dominated whenever it refuses more genuine emergencies than the attack harm it averts, and prove a targeted trust gate adds zero over-refusal on clean input. Across 840 scored episodes over three frontier models and three defenses, refuse-more caution drives over-refusal to 100 percent on two of three models for at most a 3.7-point change in attack success and yields the worst harm everywhere, whereas our trust-gating wrapper dominates the frontier (lowest harm on every model, over-refusal at or below baseline, higher containment). Provider content filters also silently perform part of the defending and must be reported separately.

title: LLM WikiLeaks: Uncovering URL-Based Capability Extension and Security Circumvention in Agentic Message Boards
abstract: Autonomous agents have been observed acting beyond their assigned tasks, accessing unauthorized systems, and establishing communication channels to exchange information, yet the Web and network-level techniques they use to extend their capabilities and circumvent security restrictions remain poorly understood. We study these techniques through the ProWiki incident, in which agents restricted to outbound HTTP GET requests repurposed a public German-language wiki as a message board. We analyze 14,591 agent edits containing 79,541 URL postings and present corroborating evidence that the published URLs reflect the agents' operational activity. We find that 26,717 URL occurrences (33.6%) embed target URLs within one to five layers of third-party Web services. By recursively reconstructing these nested URLs, we identify 67 distinct intermediate services and classify their functionality. Most intermediate layers (73.8%) extend agents' capabilities by delegating content extraction and transformation to external Web services: Markdown and OCR services convert web content into machine-readable text, JSON filtering services extract selected fields, and archival services expose historical versions of pages. The remaining 26.2% facilitate circumvention of access restrictions and evasion of detection, including CORS and fetch proxies that retrieve content on agents' behalf, and link shorteners and redirectors that hide destination URLs from mechanisms inspecting literal URLs or outer hostnames. Agents also reach the same targets through multiple URL paths, consistent with attempts to evade rate limits or obscure request origins. Our results expose a gap between the capabilities granted to agents and those they can obtain by composing publicly available Web services: restricting an agent's local toolset or direct Internet access may be insufficient while third-party services remain reachable.

title: MOFjson: An Explicit Topological Representation of Metal-Organic Frameworks for Language Models
abstract: Language models for metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) rely on formats that separate atomic geometry from structural topology, forcing models to choose between unstructured coordinate lists and non-spatial string identifiers[1]. We present MOFjson, the first representation separating structural data into a raw atomic layer with explicit bond shift vectors and a derived layer exposing secondary building units (metal nodes and organic linkers) and network topology. Additionally, we introduce a benchmark with crystal-derived ground truth across four question categories. Across four models, MOFjson beats all three baselines in every category: 100% vs. 18-47% on reaching a block's nearest periodic copy, 96% vs. 71% on crystal system characterisation, and 60% vs. 48% on metal node and organic linker coordination. Ablating shift labels drops accuracy to 12.7%, proving models read the periodic graph rather than the surface format. MOFjson gives language models structure to read rather than reconstruct, establishing a foundation for agentic tool workflows and constrained MOF generation.

title: Rethinking Verification in Agent Harnesses
abstract: Agent harnesses enable large language models to act through tools, observe the results, and iteratively work toward a task goal. Verification checks and revises agents' work to improve output quality. Yet there is limited guidance on how harnesses should organize this effort. We study verification as an axis of test-time scaling by examining when to intervene, who checks the work, and how checking leads to revision. Our framework spans four layers of the agent lifecycle: initial instructions, mid-turn reminders, completion gates, and independent review. We compare 17 designs across seven frontier coding models on Terminal-Bench (TB) and SWE-bench Verified (SWE), and introduce VisualBench for expert evaluation of visual and interactive artifacts. Initial instructions and execution-time reminders yield modest, model-dependent average gains on the coding benchmarks, without substantially increasing average output token use. Completion gates can yield larger gains but may substantially increase cost. Independent review by a critic offers a more favorable accuracy-cost tradeoff, improving average accuracy by 5.9-9.5 percentage points on TB and 3.9-6.6 on SWE at 1.13-1.25 and 1.00-1.04 times baseline cost, respectively. On VisualBench, independent review achieves net preferences of 13.2-23.8 points over the baseline across its four designs, exceeding the evaluated L0-L2 designs. Additional review rounds or independent critics further improve average TB accuracy by up to 3.5 percentage points. Together, these results provide empirical guidance for verification design in agent harnesses and support independent review as a practical axis of test-time scaling.

title: HobbyLM: A Sparse Mixture-of-Experts Model Family on a Hobby Budget
abstract: We describe HobbyLM, a family of small sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models trained from scratch with a few hundred to a few thousand dollars of rented GPU time. The core is a decoder-only transformer with fine-grained experts, sigmoid routing with auxiliary-loss-free load balancing, grouped-query attention with per-head QK-normalization, and aMuon/AdamW optimizer split. Each of these choices was selected with a single-variable ablation suite at 130M parameters. On this architecture we train a 500M-parameter model (169M active) on 40B FineWeb tokens and post-train it into a chat model, a masked-diffusion language model, a function-calling and computer-use agent, and a single "omni" checkpoint that reads text, images, video, sound and speech through frozen encoders and small projectors. We run these models on a laptop CPU with a from-scratch Rust inference engine. Two of the authors then adopted the architecture without architectural changes to build HobbyLM-1B (1.04B total, 305M active parameters), trained on a 100B-token curated mixture with a high-quality anneal. HobbyLM-1B reaches a 47.5 average on seven zero-shot benchmarks, and its builders also release an instruction-tuned model and an on-device macOS computer-use adapter. Finally, we describe HobbyLM-Image, a 333M-parameter flow-matching diffusion transformer that generates 1024x1024 images in a 32x-compressed latent space, together with a dependency-light CPU implementation of the full text-to-image pipeline. We report what worked, what did not, and where the small-scale ceilings lie. We also state for each component which author designed or built it.

title: Large Language Models: A Plain-Language Overview for Engineers
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are neural networks trained on huge text collections to generate text by predicting what comes next. Engineers using ChatGPT and other generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools need a clear picture of what training changes and prompts add. The article starts with the Transformer, which connects words in context, and pre-training, where models learn to predict text. It then explains how fine-tuning adapts models to requests, with reinforcement learning from human feedback using human answer rankings. Next, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) supplies documents, while chain-of-thought prompting encourages intermediate steps and agents use tools. FlashAttention lowers training and running costs by reducing data movement during attention; quantized low-rank adaptation (QLoRA) saves fine-tuning memory. Readers get a life cycle figure and tables comparing methods and their limits. A short checklist for judging LLM evaluation claims flags test material in training (data contamination) and model-based grading (LLM-as-a-judge). It also covers very long inputs (long context) and hallucination, meaning false or unsupported claims. Check factual accuracy separately from whether an answer sounds helpful.

title: An Agentic AI Workflow for Liver Lesion Segmentation and Structured Radiology Reporting
abstract: Despite advances in automated liver lesion segmentation, a gap remains between image-derived predictions and clinically interpretable radiology reports. Bridging this gap requires quantitative measurements that are both reproducible and traceable. We present an evidence-grounded agentic AI framework that connects liver and lesion segmentation with deterministic quantification and structured reporting. TotalSegmentator-based nnU-Net models delineate the liver, Couinaud segments, and lesions, while computational tools extract volumes, dimensions, counts, and anatomical locations. A large language model (LLM) organizes these measurements into a predefined reporting schema, with numerical consistency checks against source measurements. On 51 LiTS cases, the segmentation stage achieved a liver Dice score of 0.947, lesion sensitivity of 75.6%, and positive predictive value of 68.9%. Exploratory screening of 25,494 MERLIN reports identified 10,208 (40.0%) with liver-related abnormalities. By connecting quantitative imaging evidence with agentic report generation, this work takes a step toward human-centered medical AI that prioritizes traceability and clinical relevance.

title: Built to Remember, Shipped to Forget: Operational Contracts, Failures, and Repairs in Containerized LLM Agent Deployments
abstract: LLM agent systems reach production as container images run by platforms such as Docker, Compose, and Kubernetes. Framework and platform document opposite expectations: to the platform a container is disposable, while the framework persists conversations, pauses runs for human input, and resumes interrupted work from saved state; each side specifies only its own behavior, so the obligations their composition creates are stated nowhere. We present the first empirical study of this boundary, stating these obligations as operational contracts: guarantees a deployment must provide to preserve an agent system's required behavior when a deployment-platform event occurs. From the first-party documentation of LangGraph and the three platforms we derive 14 contracts and evaluate them with three independent sources of evidence: 433 deployed open-source agent systems, seven events induced on 12 of them, and 122 developer repairs mined from 39,261 commits, pull requests, and issues. At least one contract applies to 75.5% of the systems, yet its guarantee is routinely missing: of systems that must keep state beyond the process, 37.4% lose it to a restart and 41.5% to a container replacement, and every assessable deployment stops the framework's production server mid-drain. Induced events turn 14 of 16 predicted violations into runtime failures and all seven predicted holds pass. The failures are born in deployment but repaired in code: developer repairs independently cover twelve of the fourteen contracts, 78% change application code, and only two in three fully restore the violated guarantee. The 14-contract catalogue, detection rules, fault-injection harness, and 35-pattern repair taxonomy provide a basis for checking and strengthening agent deployments.

title: CodeMeepo: A Multi-Agent Workflow for Repository-Level Code Migration and Optimization
abstract: Repository-level code migration rewrites an entire project in a new programming language while preserving its observable behavior. It is challenging because behavior spans interdependent modules, dependencies and build infrastructure must be adapted to the target ecosystem, and the source code is often the only specification.   Large language model agents can now attempt these migrations end to end, but three challenges remain. First, an agent that writes both the translation and its acceptance tests may overlook the same requirements in both, leaving missing or incorrect behavior undetected. Second, large repositories can exceed a model's context window, and dividing the work into smaller tasks does not ensure that all required behavior is migrated. Third, even behaviorally correct translations may be slower than the original implementation.   We present CodeMeepo, a multi-agent pipeline for complete and efficient migration of large repositories. Each milestone is evaluated against a fixed external oracle that the agents neither author nor modify. A separate parity assessment compares source and target components in scope and adds identified gaps back into the plan as required work. Ordered milestones limit the scope of each task, while cumulative regression checks guard against breaking already-migrated behavior. A benchmark-guided optimization phase addresses performance, followed by full-suite conformance testing and repair. Eight specialized agent roles communicate through file artifacts, and a deterministic state machine governs repair, deferral, scope changes, and termination.   On nine subjects in three language pairs, CodeMeepo achieves the best pass rate on every subject and passes 18% more tests than a state-of-the-art multi-agent baseline using the same model. On a production daemon, its optimization phase improves half of the benchmarks, by 25% on average.

title: InferPriv: Evaluating Inferential Privacy Leakage in LLM Assistants
abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based personal agents are increasingly deployed to handle everyday tasks on users' behalf. These agents have access to private user information, while their tasks involve communicating with third parties; this raises a critical privacy concern that agents may inappropriately reveal sensitive user information to these recipients. Existing benchmarks primarily assess direct privacy leakage, where an agent explicitly states a pre-specified secret or attribute. However, they do not capture \textit{inferential leakage}, where the model leaves indirect cues in the reply that implicitly leaks sensitive attributes. We introduce \textsc{InferPriv}, a benchmark that measures whether an honest-but-curious recipient can infer a user's sensitive attributes from an LLM's reply on routine task. Evaluating five frontier models, we find that inferential leakage substantially exceeds direct leakage across models and prompts. Under a privacy-aware system prompt, GPT-6.1-Sol, Sonnet-5.5, and Gemini-3.8-Flash achieve near-zero direct leakage, yet the inferential leakage rate remains between 16.2--25.2\%. These findings suggest that evaluating explicit leakage alone can substantially understate the privacy risks.

title: An Empirical Study of Reinforcement Learning Scaling Laws
abstract: The discovery of scaling laws enables prediction of the performance, the optimal resource allocation strategy, and the best hyperparameter configuration of a large-scale training job based on inexpensive experiments at smaller scales. Guided by these empirical scaling laws, the deep learning community has achieved great success in training large (self-)supervised models on Internet-scale datasets. In contrast, despite its potential and wide application, reinforcement learning (RL) has yet to find a guiding principle for predictable scaling. In this work, we conduct an empirical study of RL scaling laws of an actor-critic algorithm in two procedurally generated environments, Starpilot and Craftax. We discover empirical scaling laws with strong predictive performance in both environments. The discovered scaling laws accurately predict the aforementioned three quantities for larger-scale training jobs up to two orders of magnitude in total training compute. In particular, we employ a variant of Elo scores for the single-agent RL paradigm as an alternative performance metric than the commonly used mean episode return. Our results show that the Elo score is a much more predictable metric than the mean episode return, making it a better choice for fitting scaling laws. By applying our discovered scaling laws to increase training compute, we establish a new state of the art in the challenging Craftax environment. Beneath the surface of the global scaling trend, we also observe a non-monotonic scaling pattern of the compute-optimal model size in Craftax. We connect this observation to a pathology known as Ray interference.

title: From Intelligence to Autonomy: Foundations and Construction of Autonomous Agents for Future Intelligent Systems
abstract: Artificial intelligence is moving from one-off perception and generation tasks toward long-term planning, tool use, and interaction with real environments. Greater task competence, however, does not automatically yield autonomy: an external actor may still have to set goals, sustain operating conditions, detect failures, and approve updates. We define an autonomous agent as a system that, within explicit identity and authority boundaries, maintains both task goals and viability conditions, acts continuously using models of the world and itself, and adjusts its control mechanisms and long-term capabilities through feedback. We trace the conceptual path from homeostasis and feedback control to autopoiesis and biological autonomy. We then distinguish six lines of operationalization: computational autopoiesis, behavior-based robotics, agent formalization, adaptive software, embodied adaptation, and robotic self-modeling. On this basis, we propose a one-boundary, four-loop framework in which Operational, Viability, Reflexive, and Learning loops organize task execution, self-maintenance, metacontrol, and governed learning. Five paired simulation experiments test permission constraints, road-closure response, health maintenance, capability re-estimation, and cross-task learning. Their results provide preliminary evidence for the feasibility of these mechanisms, while broader environments and physical systems remain to be tested.

title: MOTIO: Agentic Skill Engineering for Reality-Grounded Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
abstract: We present MOTIO, an agentic skill-engineering system that turns ordinary human-action videos, reality-grounded 3D assets, motion references, and reusable robot skills into executable humanoid loco-manipulation programs. Through in-context task and contact reasoning, an agent constructs staged robot-native interactions and improves them using physics execution, multi-frame feedback, and human validation---without task-specific teleoperation or robot demonstration collection. Agentic 3D supplies metric product and environment assets, while existing whole-body, inverse-kinematics, and dexterous-hand interfaces realize the programs. Across 33 timestamped first approvals, the median recorded agent-turn time is 97.0 minutes and request-to-approval duration is 2.80 hours. Simulation-side layout and object variation prepare a long-horizon bottle-disposal skill for a continuous 101.75-second physical G1 execution in a scanned office; physical refinement reduces screw-tightening thread residual by 76.0%. Agent-generated skills additionally supervise BC/DAgger distillation into one shared reference policy, completing 18 simulated tasks under the same checkpoint without inference-time expert intervention. Project page: https://iiiiqiiii.github.io/motio/

title: LegoSR: A Unified Framework for Self-improving Agent-Guided Scientific Discovery
abstract: Equation discovery solvers often use different data interfaces, equation representations and evaluation criteria, making their results difficult to compare. We present LegoSR, a unified framework for algebraic symbolic regression and differential equation discovery. LegoSR integrates seven solvers through a common equation representation and evaluation process, and supports searches constrained by partially known equations. Researchers can run solvers directly or use LegoSR Agent, which selects solvers and adapts searches based on solver knowledge, intermediate results and lessons from earlier tasks. On noisy ordinary and partial differential equation benchmarks, LegoSR Agent recovers nearly as many equations as the union of seven expert-tuned solvers and outperforms a generic agent with the same model, tools and budget by up to 29 percentage points. Three examples demonstrate basic use, adaptive solver selection and discovery guided by partial physical knowledge.

title: ReSight: Task-Driven Self-Improving Memory for Embodied Agents
abstract: Robots can use historical observations to answer spatiotemporal queries in familiar environments, but the presence of relevant evidence does not imply that existing tools support the operations a task requires. We introduce ReSight, a task-driven self-improving memory system for embodied agents that expands the capabilities for processing and accessing historical observations as task demands arise. ReSight retains keyframes and their spatiotemporal associations, separating observation evidence from extensible derived fields so that stored observations can be reprocessed for new needs. An execution agent and a coding agent share this memory through different interfaces: the former calls registered tools within a bounded online budget, while the latter uses a programmable workspace and a larger exploration budget to inspect evidence, write programs, and acquire models as needed. To realize capability expansion in ReSight, we develop Explore-Distill-Mount (EDM), which identifies capability gaps from execution and exploration records without task reference answers and converts exploration-derived solutions into reusable memory builders, query tools, and skills, extending memory representations and access capabilities as needed. Experiments on three public benchmarks demonstrate effective base memory access and capability expansion. With the execution model and online budget held fixed within each benchmark, EDM reduces mean position error on OC-NaVQA from 33.10 m to 24.72 m and improves high-level success on FindingDory from 38.3% to 63.8%. With the tools and skill frozen, success still improves by 28.3 percentage points on FindingDory episodes excluded from exploration and distillation. Experiments on real robot patrol memories further demonstrate reuse of these capabilities for subsequent queries and new memories, with fewer online tool calls on average.

title: SkillShift-Bench: Benchmarking Skill Learning under Environment Evolution for Web Agents
abstract: Skill learning enables web agents to reuse prior experience for long-horizon interactive tasks. However, learned skills are typically evaluated in closed environments, overlooking the fact that real-world web deployment involves continuous shifts in invocation context, perceptual grounding, and execution feasibility. To this end, we introduce SkillShift-Bench, the first benchmark for evaluating skill learning with controlled open-environment shifts. SkillShift-Bench simulates Contextual Shift, Perceptual Shift, and Execution Shift across three self-hosted web systems, and evaluates agents with diagnostics covering task success, interaction cost, skill use, and skill failure. Comprehensive experiments reveal systematic robustness degradation under controlled shifts, characterized by lower success rates, higher interaction costs, and more frequent skill failures, with Execution Shift exerting the strongest pressure. We further formulate shifted skill execution as a nonstationary local executability problem and provide both a dynamic-regret analysis and a practical test-time adaptation method, demonstrating the feasibility of improving learned-skill execution without relearning the skill library. Code, tasks, environments, documentation, and the leaderboard are available at https://skillshift-bench.github.io/.

title: Trajectory2Gym: Decision-Grounded Compositional Interaction Synthesis for Tool-Use Agents
abstract: Successful tool-use trajectories are not necessarily useful supervision. Even successful interactions may underrepresent multi-step dependencies or contain actions that are unjustified by the information visible to the agent at decision time. We identify two coupled requirements for effective trajectory supervision: compositional coverage, so that important observation-action dependencies are represented, and decision grounding, so that each supervised action is supported by the learner-visible interaction history. We introduce Trajectory2Gym, which constructs executable interactions around under-supported compositional structures and derives supervision only from grounded decisions in their realized executions. Structural-support selection allocates the resulting experience, while parent-normalized supervised fine-tuning preserves the semantic interaction as the unit of training weight. This reframes trajectory generation as the deliberate construction of learnable interaction experience, rather than the collection of successful trajectories. Across five Qwen3 scales, Trajectory2Gym improves Tau1, Tau2, and BFCL at every tested scale, increasing the equal-weight three-benchmark mean by 16.9-29.8 percentage points. The gains are strongest in stateful and multi-turn interaction, where later decisions depend on earlier observations and feedback. Our results suggest that scaling tool-use agents depends not only on collecting more successful trajectories, but on constructing interactions whose dependencies are represented and whose decisions are learnable from the agent's visible history.

title: Replicate What Varies: Resource Sharing for Domain-Randomized Embodied Simulation
abstract: Simulation provides a low-cost sandbox where embodied agents can attempt tasks, observe outcomes, and learn from experience. Running many diverse simulation environments concurrently can consume substantial CPU and GPU memory because independently constructed scenes duplicate resources that remain unchanged across instances. We present Patchwork, a resource-sharing system for domain-randomized simulation, built around the representation $E=T+Δ$: a shared template contains common resources, and a patch records the mutations needed to construct a target environment. Patchwork separates randomization sampling from replay and selects reusable templates together with patches that preserve each target environment's intended configuration. Its layered runtime shares compiled model structure and immutable assets while keeping mutable parameters and simulation state private to each instance. We implement Patchwork on robosuite and MuJoCo and evaluate it on LIBERO-plus and RoboCasa365 workloads. At 32 replicas, shared-template execution reduces CPU RSS by 88-92% relative to process-per-environment execution. Controlled experiments show how sharing shifts memory growth toward template diversity and unique asset content rather than instance count, within the supported sharing boundaries.

title: HA-DiPO: Diffusion Policy Optimization for Heterogeneous Cooperative Transport
abstract: Cooperative transport with heterogeneous legged robots requires coordinating different motion capabilities while supporting an unfixed shared payload. We present HA-DiPO (Heterogeneous-Agent Diffusion Policy Optimization), a hierarchical multi-agent reinforcement learning framework under centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE). The framework decouples team-level coordination from embodiment-specific motion control: at the high level, a centralized critic uses team-value estimates to jointly train independent coordination policies, aligning robot-specific action responses with a shared transport objective; at the low level, embodiment-specific robust motion policies track the coordination commands. The high-level diffusion policies offer more flexible action distributions than single-Gaussian parameterizations, allowing potentially multimodal coordination responses to be represented. The coordination policies learn from scratch through reward-driven simulator interaction without demonstrations. At execution, each robot generates coordination commands using only local robot and payload observations, without partner-state inputs or inter-robot messages. Simulation comparisons show that HA-DiPO achieves higher final mean returns and velocity-tracking success rates, as well as lower velocity errors, than the evaluated baselines. Real-world experiments further demonstrate quadrupedal-wheeled-legged and human-robot cooperative transport.

title: SWE-Ladder: Learning to Localize, Reproduce, and Patch via Progressive Privileged Self-Distillation
abstract: Resolving a repository-level issue typically requires a software-engineering (SWE) agent to localize the faulty code, reproduce the failure, and patch the code. Reinforcement learning trains such agents from a single test result on the final patch, while on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) adds token-level supervision from a teacher with privileged evidence, exposing the full reference patch at every step. Neither provides stage-specific guidance for localization or reproduction. We propose SWE-Ladder, which turns the verified repair of each training instance into stage-specific evidence: the changed files and lines for localization, the fail-to-pass tests for reproduction, and the diff for patching. A rule-based router assigns each step of an end-to-end rollout to a stage based on its tool call, a frozen teacher sees only the matching evidence, and the stages are distilled in repair order while GRPO optimizes the full trajectory. With Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 on SWE-bench Verified under the R2E-Gym scaffold, SWE-Ladder improves pass@1 from 9.6% to 16.4%, compared with 10.4% for GRPO and 12.4% for OPSD with the full patch. Under the OpenHands scaffold, it improves pass@1 from 13.0% to 17.6%. Reversing the stage order under R2E-Gym reduces pass@1 to 11.4%.

title: PACE: Research Proving Agent for Adaptive Conjecture Exploration
abstract: Many mathematical research agents focus on solving problems with fixed statements. However, conjecture research, especially in applied mathematics, may require revising candidate questions or conclusions as investigation proceeds, coupling problem formulation with proof development. We present PACE, a research-proof agent that supports this process through a structured research loop that selects mathematical objectives and develops or challenges candidate mechanisms. The whole prover constructs proofs from these mechanisms, and an independent verifier checks them against the original target. Evidence-tracking memory stores assumptions and dependencies arising during research and marks evidence for revalidation when a candidate or condition changes. This memory supports task-specific context composition that keeps checked premises, exploratory material and unresolved obligations distinct. To evaluate proof construction and conjecture research, we introduce ResearchProofBench, an applied-mathematics benchmark focused on optimization, comprising 51 known-proof tasks with 331 hidden checkpoints under historical abstract access and six open-problem cases. The known-proof tasks assess reconstruction of published results, while the open-problem cases assess mathematical investigation and proof development. On the 51 known-proof tasks, PACE achieves an aggregate Proof Score of 75.16 and completes 20 proofs. In conjecture research, PACE develops conditional results, with its submissions receiving higher review scores than the compared baselines.

title: Seeing the Options: Typed Decisions over Visual Candidates with Reusable Option Memory
abstract: Typed decision-making tasks in agents, such as UI element selection, product recommendation, and chart matching, require models to choose from a set of discrete candidates. While prior work demonstrates that text-only System One models achieve four key properties including candidate-order invariance, scalability, and cache reuse via separate request-candidate encoding, extending them to multimodal settings where candidates are visual remains underexplored. We introduce Iris, a framework that accommodates image, text, or hybrid candidates while preserving the core decision module. We prove that order invariance and exact cache reuse hold for any per-candidate encoder under Iris, and derive the closed-form latency reduction. We construct a visual-candidate benchmark from Multimodal-Mind2Web (K=16, deduplicated, order-shuffled, three generalization splits). Independent encoding (Iris) achieves 78.4 / 72.1 / 74.8 percent accuracy with zero-flip rate under candidate reordering. Joint encoding reaches 90.6 / 89.5 / 91.6 percent but suffers an 8 to 10 percent answer-flip rate when shuffled. To bridge this gap, we propose a design that encodes each candidate conditioned on the request state without inter-candidate cross-attention; it preserves strict order invariance, enables forked cache sharing, and attains 91.7 / 86.5 / 90.0 percent accuracy at one-third of OneJev latency with calibrated null probabilities (AUROC 0.93 to 0.97). Reusing image candidates across requests cuts latency by 37x at K=256 and 191x at K=2048. On MetaEncoder benchmarks, Iris-4B achieves 100 percent on JevBench original and easy, outperforming 30B MetaEncoder and 27B OpenJev. Finally, we resolve a systems bottleneck on Ampere GPUs: reformulating Qwen3.5 patch-embedding Conv3d into its exact matrix-product form accelerates processing by 350x. Code, data, and checkpoints: https://github.com/lllfx/Iris.

title: Human-Feedback-Guided Multi-Agent Inverse Reinforcement Learning for Interactive Driving Behavior Modeling
abstract: Modeling human driving behavior is fundamental to understanding driver decision-making and supporting autonomous vehicles (AVs) in mixed traffic. Reward learning offers a principled way to infer the latent objectives behind driving behaviors, yet most existing methods are formulated in single-agent settings and treat surrounding vehicles as dynamic obstacles. Directly extending reward learning to multi-agent scenarios is difficult because the joint action space grows exponentially with the number of interacting vehicles. In addition, existing approaches mainly rely on physical demonstrations and rarely exploit human feedback during reward recovery. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a Human-Feedback-Guided Multi-Agent Inverse Reinforcement Learning (HFG-MAIRL) framework for interactive driving behavior modeling. First, we develop a multi-agent maximum-entropy inverse reinforcement learning module that explicitly models each vehicle and its directly interacting neighbors in a localized Markov game, while using aggregated traffic states to capture the influence of the broader traffic environment. The resulting coupled multi-vehicle responses are approximated through finite marginal-response iterations over factorized vehicle-level policies, avoiding explicit enumeration of the full joint action space. Second, we incorporate human feedback as ordinal preference supervision through a Bradley-Terry likelihood. In our experiments, driver emotion labels are used as one instantiation of such feedback and converted into pairwise ordinal preference constraints. Experiments on the AIDE dataset show that HFG-MAIRL outperforms representative IRL baselines in decision modeling and produces interpretable feedback-aligned reward patterns.

title: ProtAgent: Post-Training Compact Protein Tool Agents with Interaction-Level Credit Assignment
abstract: Protein annotation agents must choose suitable bioinformatics tools, interpret their outputs, and use the resulting evidence in the final answer. Most existing systems rely on frontier-scale models. We ask whether a compact model can instead learn this behavior through post-training with real tool interaction. We present ProtAgent, a two-stage pipeline that uses supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to learn the tool interface and standard on-policy REINFORCE to improve the interaction policy. Intermediate tool calls receive action rewards, and the final response receives a terminal answer reward. Step-level returns assign these rewards to the responses that produced them and to preceding actions. The episode-level baseline instead assigns one episode return to every action. On a fixed closed-loop protocol with real bioinformatics tools, ProtAgent-8B achieves 61.00% success under the annotation-coverage metric, compared with 41.60% for DeepSeek-V3.2-Thinking 671B and 60.80% for the strongest evaluated frontier system. In the three-seed comparison, mean success is 42.70% with episode-level returns and 61.40% with step-level returns under identity return normalization; the corresponding group-relative results are 36.50% and 58.20%. The metric measures recovery of reference annotations under this protocol; it does not by itself establish biological correctness or complete evidence grounding.

title: Memory or a Clock? Auditing a Memory Advantage in XLand-MiniGrid with Seeds, Maps and Evaluation Noise Apart
abstract: On a partially observable XLand-MiniGrid task, an LSTM agent beats a memory-free MLP by 25 percentage points. The gap looks like a clear case of memory. We ask two questions about it. First, how much of a measured gap is noise? Separating training seed, map and evaluation randomness in 60 runs, each re-evaluated three times, we find that about ten paired seeds detect a 10-point gap in final success. The binary "task acquired" verdict, a common summary of learning curves, is 76% evaluation noise and would need about a hundred seeds for the same gap. Second, is the gap memory? On a sealed panel of new maps, opened once, a memory-free MLP of the LSTM's size comes within 3.3 points of the LSTM when it is given the time step, and gains no measurable benefit from its width without it. With the time step, an MLP a quarter of the LSTM's size, and the LSTM with its state erased at every step, also come within about 5 points. A linear probe reads the time step from the trained LSTM's state. On this task, most of the apparent memory advantage is an advantage of knowing the time, which matters because episodes are cut at a fixed limit and the reward shrinks with time. We recommend giving memory-free baselines the time step, and we release the protocol, the event-driven tooling and every checkpoint.

title: Agentic Digital Twin-Assisted Multimodal Predictive Handover
abstract: Rapid mobility, blockage, and propagation changes can invalidate instantaneous handover decisions in dense mid-band and millimeter-wave (mmWave) networks. We therefore propose a flexible, model-agnostic \emph{Agentic Digital Twin (DT)} framework for predictive cell handover. The DT generates synchronized multimodal states, while three agents autonomously select forecasts, plan handover actions, and adapt decisions using execution feedback. The proposed Agentic DT provided the best collective balance among handover activity, the reliability of the selected links, and the accuracy of target next-generation Node B (gNB) selection relative to the best available future link. It reduced average handovers from $11.0$ for Event~A3 to $8.0$ per trajectory while maintaining   $98.2\%$ ray-path availability.

title: Approximate Universal Prediction under Interaction
abstract: Bayesian mixtures, and Solomonoff induction in particular, provide an idealized model of prediction learned by minimizing population log loss, and they underlie universal agents such as AIXI. An agent that plans with an approximation of such a predictor decides where that predictor is evaluated, and a planner can be drawn toward branches on which its model is optimistic. We study which approximation guarantees survive this feedback. For normalized finite-horizon causal mixtures, the transfer coefficient factors into a policy likelihood ratio and task evidence available before each prediction, so task rarity and action-branch rarity can compound. Within one fixed universal mixture, infinitely many computable environments admit excess prediction error of order $κη\,2^{K(μ)}$, where $η$ is the training KL budget and $κ$ measures policy coverage. This order is sharp, and for each target a computable predictor attains it at a suitable finite horizon, so computability alone does not remove the penalty. For bounded returns, value error is controlled by the probability of entering a poorly covered branch plus a square-root term in $η$. Both terms are necessary, and finite maximum coverage ratios are not required. Motivated by the mentor override of Golden Handcuffs, we derive margins for preserving deferral decisions and conditional KL budgets with an unavoidable inverse-history-probability penalty, and a counterexample separates agreement of deferral decisions from task-wise event avoidance. The guarantees apply to any predictor architecture that meets explicit population approximation and coverage conditions, which gives concrete targets for implementing idealized universal agents.

title: ArchGuard-APR: Architecture-Constraint-Aware Multi-Agent Program Repair Using Repository Graphs and Execution Feedback
abstract: Repository-level automated program repair must reason about more than a localized failing statement. A candidate change can satisfy a narrow test while violating dependency boundaries, modifying an unsafe path, or relying on context that omits relevant repository structure. ArchGuard-APR is an architecture-aware repair prototype that integrates deterministic repository analysis, immutable repository graphs, explicit architecture profiles, graph-guided context retrieval, role-based repair orchestration, patch-policy enforcement, isolated execution feedback, provider cost controls, and canonical source-free evidence.   We evaluate the implemented pipeline through an exploratory paired feasibility study, not a confirmatory effectiveness experiment. Six executions were planned; four completed, and two black-4 conditions ended in pre-provider infrastructure attrition. Across two valid paired tasks, baseline and ArchGuard conditions each produced 0/2 successful repairs, and all four completed outputs were classified as invalid patches.   The completed executions consumed 35,431 input tokens and 2,737 output tokens, for a total of 38,168 tokens, at a total cost of USD 0.1296325. No effectiveness advantage was observed, and the sample provides no useful inferential basis. The study instead establishes the engineering feasibility of composing architecture constraints with a reproducible repair pipeline and identifies patch validity and infrastructure robustness as the principal targets for future work.

title: Numina Fuse: Interactive Autoformalization in Lean 4
abstract: Numina Fuse is an agent-native application for formalizing mathematics in Lean 4. Since Lean can compile while not representing its intended informal meaning, and agents now write Lean faster than people can read it, we built Fuse around human supervision of agent work. A user works with an AI orchestrator on a Lean project and supervises it through views of the blueprint, the dependency graph, and the Lean code, while the backend keeps the project's derived state and runs agents for hours without the user present. We describe the development of Fuse throughout 2026, as it moved from a prescribed pipeline of agents paced by human review to an orchestrator that dispatches specialists, provers, and parallel children on its own. We designed for this shift, keeping project state, tooling, and interface design separate from orchestration so that agents could take over more of the work as models improved. We report Fuse's use in a formalization of the three-dimensional Kakeya conjecture and a study of prover models. We close with lessons for the next generation of autoformalization systems. Fuse Desktop, an open-source local version, is available at https://github.com/project-numina/fuse-desktop.

title: Securing Edge & Physical AI: Post-Quantum IoT Blockchain for Mission-Critical Cyber-Physical Agents
abstract: Distributed Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS) and Edge AI networks increasingly depend on public-key authentication and key-establishment mechanisms that are vulnerable to cryptographically relevant Quantum Computers (QC). Shor's algorithm threatens widely deployed asymmetric primitives, while Grover's algorithm reduces the effective security margins of symmetric and hash-based mechanisms. Although Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) provides a migration path, its larger public keys, ciphertexts, and signatures introduce additional computation, memory, communication, storage, and packet-fragmentation costs that can constrain dynamic multi-agent systems. In this article, we introduce rotational secrecy, an architectural objective that limits temporal key exposure through authenticated transitions between cryptographic epochs. We present Private Authentication for Rotational Secrecy (PARS), a reference mechanism that coordinates policy-triggered key establishment, rotation, and reconciliation among authorized Physical AI agents. For deployments that need distributed agreement on security state, we further develop the PARS-Enabled Edge Security Ledger (PARS-ESL), an optional permissioned architecture maintained by authorized validators or capable edge gateways. PARS-ESL does not store high-volume operational transactions. Instead, it records authenticated state for key epochs, group membership, revocation, algorithm-suite policies, challenge validation, and recovery checkpoints. As a result, resource-constrained agents can take part as lightweight clients, and low-latency operational traffic stays outside the ledger consensus path, protected by the currently active symmetric epoch keys. Our results show that ledger-assisted post-quantum key-epoch management is feasible for selected Edge AI and CPS security-control workloads under the stated trust, compromise, connectivity, and resource assumptions.

title: Human-Aware Agentic Driving: Rethinking Driver State, Trust, and Intervention
abstract: Agentic driving brings goal-directed reasoning, memory, tools, and adaptive interaction into automated vehicles. A vehicle can clarify a request, explain a maneuver, or prepare a driver to take control, then adapt its next action to the response. These capabilities make the vehicle an active participant in shaping the human behavior it observes. We examine how agentic interaction affects driver-state inference, trust and reliance, and human intervention in conditional automation. Established findings on attention, takeover prediction, trust-aware planning, and adaptive warnings provide useful foundations, but their applicability depends on how observations are elicited and how assistance changes the driving task. We distinguish what remains applicable, what changes under flexible interaction, and what remains unresolved across these three areas. The analysis identifies three research priorities: establishing the effects of interventions, jointly designing interaction and driving policies, and maintaining useful adaptation across repeated use and system changes. Progress should be measured through driver comprehension, appropriate reliance, and the ability to perform the required driving action in time.

title: AgentOrch: How Close Can Global Orchestration Come to Step-by-Step Interaction?
abstract: Enterprise workflow agents typically rely on step-by-step interaction (Step-by-Step): the agent executes an action, observes its result, and invokes a large language model (LLM) again to decide the next step. Global orchestration (Global) instead generates a complete executable workflow in advance and executes it without further LLM calls, substantially reducing inference overhead, but it remains less accurate than Step-by-Step. We study how close Global can come to Step-by-Step and what narrows the remaining gap. We introduce AgentOrch, a benchmark that directly compares global orchestration with step-by-step interaction on 650 enterprise SOPs and 3,220 runtime variants under matched tools, environments, and evaluation. Step-by-Step remains more accurate for every evaluated model, but the gap has shrunk by about 79% from early models to the strongest recent model. We identify three routes to further narrowing this gap. Incremental workflow construction improves Global accuracy by an average of 9.98 percentage points (pp) without runtime execution feedback. Revising complete workflows with execution feedback improves all evaluated models, including 6.13 pp on held-out runtime variants. Targeted training on complete workflows improves accuracy by an average of 12.18 pp across all five trained models. Although a gap remains, global orchestration offers a promising path toward enterprise agents that deliver higher accuracy with fewer LLM calls.

title: Fast Instinct, Slow Reason: A Dual-Speed Agentic Framework for Self-Configuring Multi-Object Tracking in Satellite Video
abstract: Multi-object tracking in satellite video underpins persistent monitoring, yet offline-tuned trackers lack the onboard intelligence and efficiency to adapt within an observation of tens of seconds. The root is that adaptation still means relabelling and retraining the detector, which cannot run on board in time. Tuning the tracker configuration strongly controls accuracy without touching the network, yet search needs labelled or proxy evaluations, and a language agent costs seconds and tokens per decision. We propose a dual-speed agentic framework pairing a fast instinct compiled offline with a slow reason serving the mission. Its algorithm, Arbitration of Unlabelled Shortlists from Prior Experience, or AUSPEX, learns a covering shortlist and a label-free ranker from labelled source tasks and commits one configuration per sequence. Its system, a Cascaded Onboard Runtime with Verified Uplinked Skills, or CORVUS, cascades reflex, skill, and agent layers, so that a verified skill commits 2.5 s into each observation while a language agent serves natural- language missions. On SatMTB and SatVideoDT with three recent detectors, AUSPEX raises IDF1 by 2.84 to 2.94 points and MOTA by 3.21 to 3.29 points on average without target labels, balances accuracy and labels best among sixteen methods, and loses at most 0.28 IDF1 points at 1.25 tracking passes. CORVUS executes four missions with execution accuracy up to 0.99 and target recall at the perception ceiling, spends no token on the routine decision, runs on Jetson Xavier NX, and hosts fifteen language models from six families without altering any commitment, demonstrating its extensibility and generalization.

title: ConMem: Counterfactual Multi-Scenario Probing for Resolving LLM Memory Misalignment
abstract: Long-term memory is critical for autonomous Large Language Model (LLM) agents executing multi-session, long-horizon tasks. However, existing memories often inappropriately store, retain, or retrieve over-generalized, misattributed, or privacy-sensitive information, a problem we term memory misalignment. To study this problem, we construct \textbf{MemAlign}, a benchmark comprising 1,079 curated memory cases grounded in synthetic, validated multi-session conversational contexts covering diverse misalignment taxonomies. We then propose ConMem, an algorithm that reframes retention decisions as prospective counterfactual causal inference. \textbf{ConMem} synthesizes counterfactual interaction scenarios to prospectively audit downstream intervention effects across three aspects: relevant task execution, irrelevant invariance checks, and risk-sensitive boundary shifts. Experiments show that ConMem outperforms other methods, achieving 75.16\% accuracy, 64.15\% balanced accuracy, and a Macro-F1 of 65.31\%, effectively mitigating over-retention biases without sacrificing personalization utility.

title: LLMs in Cloud: A Discussion on Architecture, Orchestration, and Inference
abstract: The widespread deployment of foundational Large Language Models (LLM) across cloud datacenters marks a fundamental paradigm shift from stateless deep learning toward distributed, memory-intensive generative workloads. However, serving massive foundation models under stringent Service Level Objectives (SLO) exposes critical physical and system bottlenecks. These challenges include the persistent High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) wall, operational asymmetry between compute-bound prefilling and memory-bandwidth-bound decoding, explosive Key-Value (KV) cache expansion, prohibitive serverless cold starts, and hardware reliability vulnerabilities. Existing literature reviews remain layer-siloed, decoupling low-level accelerator virtualization from cluster orchestration and runtime inference, while largely overlooking defining advancements from 2024 to 2026. To address these limitations, this study presents a comprehensive, cross-layer systematic review guided by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 framework. We synthesize a holistic taxonomy unifying hardware virtualization, cluster-level scheduling, and runtime inference optimizations, including iteration-level continuous batching, prefill-decoding disaggregation, and hierarchical KV cache offloading. Furthermore, we evaluate resilient cloud-native service architectures, examining scale-to-zero serverless paradigms, fault-tolerant checkpointing against silent data corruption, and hardware-enforced Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) for multi-tenant isolation. Finally, we formalize the multi-dimensional Pareto trade-offs governing throughput, latency, monetary cost, and confidentiality, outlining a forward-looking research roadmap spanning Compute Express Link (CXL) memory pooling, in-memory computing, and autonomous multi-agent control planes to guide future cloud LLM infrastructure.

title: From Instructions to Exploits: Applying Program Analysis to Malicious Agent Skills Across Natural Language and Code
abstract: LLM-powered agents increasingly rely on third-party skills that combine natural-language instructions with executable code, creating supply-chain risks that may span both artifacts. Existing skill scanners often rely on rule matching or direct LLM judgments and provide limited support for tracing such cross-domain behavior. We present the Supply-Chain Scanner for Agent Skills (SCS), a static analysis framework that unifies instructions and code for security analysis. SCS compiles natural-language instructions into a constrained Python-style intermediate representation using a limited set of security-oriented APIs. It then constructs program dependence graphs for instructions and bundled code and connects them into a cross-domain graph (xPDG). A Trust-Sensitivity-Capability (TSC) model propagates security properties over the graph to support structured, largely deterministic risk detection. On a manually verified benchmark of 117 malicious and 117 benign skills, SCS achieves the highest average accuracy (85.6%), recall (95.2%), and F1-score (86.9%) among evaluated methods across five LLMs, with 80.2% precision and average token consumption of 13.7 million. Its NL-to-IR compiler achieves 92.5%-94.5% step-level correctness on 400 human-annotated instruction steps. Finally, analyzing 66,157 real-world ClawHub skills yields 2,473 candidates, of which 627 are confirmed malicious through auxiliary dynamic validation and manual review.

title: Can Agentic Code Review Catch Vulnerabilities Before They Are Merged?
abstract: LLM agents have been increasingly adopted for security-focused code review, but existing benchmarks mostly derive the reviewed changes from their later fixes instead of the real-world bug-introducing commits. In this paper, we present SecPRBench, the first comprehensive benchmark for evaluating agentic security review on validated real-world code changes. More specifically, we have built an automated agentic pipeline to autonomously harvest, build, and validate massive real-world bug-introducing commits for popular software systems. To ensure precise evaluation, we also adopt LLM-as-a-judge to credit the findings matching ground-truth vulnerabilities. To date, we have collected 265 tasks from nine critical systems, including Firefox, V8, and OpenSSL with millions of lines of code. Across eight frontier models, recall ranges from 32.5% to 78.1%, with Grok 4.6 and GPT-6 sol ranking at the top. Our study also shows that most misses are not simply oversights: in 68% of them, the agent reports on a file that holds the flaw but argues for a different mechanism. Security-focused harnesses also behave differently: OpenAI's Codex Security lowers recall by 8.3 points, mostly by abstaining, while Anthropic's Defending Code harness raises it by 7.7 points, at a higher cost.

title: FraudSociety: A Generative Agent-Based Society for the Financial-Fraud Economy
abstract: Financial fraud caused over \$15.9 billion in losses in the United States in 2025, according to the Federal Trade Commission~\citep{ftc2026databook}. Understanding such large-scale harm requires jointly modeling informational and financial dynamics. Yet existing simulators typically capture only one side of this interaction, leaving a gap in modeling how fraud unfolds in the real world. To bridge this gap, we introduce \textsc{FraudSociety}, the first LLM-agent-based simulator that jointly models these coupled dynamics. It integrates a dynamic social environment for information exposure and communication, persistent financial ledgers that preserve payment and loss histories, and a Need-Intent-Action architecture for civilian decision making. Fraudsters further adapt their communication and financial actions to individual interaction histories and ledger states, forming a closed feedback loop between the two dynamics. We validate \textsc{FraudSociety} across macro-level outcomes, micro-level behavior, and intervention effects. At the macro level, the simulated fraud outcomes closely match real-world patterns across multiple key statistics. At the micro level, it reproduces strong loss concentration, with the top 10\% of victimization records accounting for 81.1\% of total losses, consistent with Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre statistics~\citep{cafc2025annual}. Counter-fraud experiments further reveal variation across intervention strategies, with the best-performing personalized intervention reducing the repeat-payment rate from 49.4\% to 10.9\%. These results establish \textsc{FraudSociety} as both a high-fidelity simulator and a scalable testbed for evaluating anti-fraud strategies under diverse intervention conditions, thereby advancing research on financial fraud and its prevention.

title: CoEvolve: Counterfactual-Guided Co-Evolution of Memory and Collaboration in Multi-Agent Systems
abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across diverse tasks. Yet their memory and collaboration architectures often remain static, constraining continued adaptation and improvement over time. Recent work addresses this limitation by evolving memory or collaboration based on interaction experience. However, updates to these interdependent components are not necessarily aligned: an evolved workflow may require experience that memory does not provide, while evolved memory may encode guidance that the workflow cannot use. To address this problem, we propose CoEvolve, a skill-centered framework for aligned memory--collaboration evolution. CoEvolve represents reusable local collaboration patterns as skills that link evolving collaboration decisions to their supporting memories. It further compares original and counterfactual trajectories to identify local evolution signals, which coordinate updates to the skill library, skill memory, and executor memories across rounds. Experiments on the ALFWorld and WebShop benchmarks confirm that CoEvolve achieves the best overall performance among the evaluated baselines, while ablation studies further validate the effectiveness of aligned co-evolution and counterfactual-guided evolution.

title: Auditing evaluation artifacts and data leakage in large language model systems for rare disease diagnosis
abstract: Augmented large language model (LLM) systems have reported high benchmark accuracies in rare disease diagnosis, yet their real-world clinical utility remains unproven. A recent meta-analysis flagged augmented LLM diagnostic evaluations as having a high risk of bias due to suspected data leakage; however, the precise impact of these vulnerabilities on model inference has yet to be fully quantified. In this study, we present a comprehensive empirical audit to quantify evaluation artifacts across prevailing AI paradigms, using a repository of over 60,000 cases from diverse public and independent clinical cohorts. By reconstructing a state-of-the-art agentic framework, we demonstrate that candidate-space contamination artificially inflates performance: enforcing strict cross-dataset isolation resulted in a marked performance decline, with the cross-dataset mean Recall@1 decreasing from 54.3% (under conventional one-vs-rest evaluation) to 40.3% (Hedges' g = 0.94). Similar spatial overfitting in supervised classifiers caused diagnostic accuracy to drop from an internal mean of 42.9% to 16.7% across external cohorts (Cohen's d = 2.01). Furthermore, we quantify how LLMs infer diagnoses by exploiting retrospective therapeutic cues in clinical narratives, and how temporal misalignment in foundational knowledge bases leads to performance fluctuations. We conclude that prevailing evaluation protocols for augmented LLM systems inadvertently reflect data leakage rather than genuine medical reasoning. To address these systematic artifacts, we propose a rigorous evaluation framework - coupling strict data-isolation protocols with standardized benchmarking safeguards - to ensure future diagnostic AI for rare diseases is evaluated on actual clinical robustness.

title: A Tool-Grounded AI Agent for Gauge Coupling Unification and Proton Decay
abstract: We present proton_agent, a tool-grounded AI agent that enables natural-language interaction with computational tools for gauge coupling unification and proton decay in grand unified theories. The agent translates user requests into computational tasks, selects and executes the appropriate tools, and interprets their outputs. All numerical calculations, model evaluations, experimental comparisons, parameter scans, and visualizations are handled by a deterministic scientific backend to ensure numerical accuracy and reproducibility. A central objective of this framework is to enable fully local deployment using free and open-source LLMs, while retaining compatibility with commercial LLM APIs. The framework computes one- and two-loop gauge beta coefficients for user-defined scalar and fermion multiplets and performs gauge coupling evolution through the Standard Model and various intermediate symmetry-breaking stages of $SO(10)$, including $SU(3)_C \times SU(2)_L \times SU(2)_R \times U(1)_{B-L}$, $SU(3)_C \times SU(2)_L \times U(1)_R \times U(1)_{B-L}$, $SU(4)_C \times SU(2)_L \times U(1)_R$, and $SU(4)_C \times SU(2)_L \times SU(2)_R$. For proton decay, the framework evaluates gauge-mediated dimension-six contributions in non-supersymmetric $SU(5)$ and $SO(10)$, as well as dressed dimension-five contributions in their supersymmetric counterparts. It supports benchmark calculations for user-specified parameter points, random and grid-based parameter scans, Markov-chain Monte Carlo exploration, comparisons with experimental limits, and publication-ready two- and three-dimensional visualizations. We describe the agent architecture, demonstrate its capabilities through representative benchmark calculations and regression tests, and discuss its current physics scope.

title: Data Governance for Generative and Agentic AI : Technology, Law, Economics, and Security
abstract: This book develops a unified governance framework for systems that retrieve, generate, infer, remember and act on information from large language models and retrieval augmented pipelines to autonomous multi agent systems. Eleven chapters and eight appendices integrate three disciplinary lenses-technology, law and economics-across the full lifecycle: data quality, lineage and provenance; global data protection law and intellectual property; the economics of data governance; digital trust, cybersecurity and zero-trust architecture; ethics and responsible AI; governing generative AI pipelines; governing agentic AI and multi-agent systems; data governance in elections and the public sphere; AI regulation across six jurisdictions; and the design of a governance control plane for 2030. Each chapter is anchored in Indian law and institutions while maintaining a comparative, cross jurisdictional perspective.

title: RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement with Human Feedback
abstract: Can AI agents autonomously train useful language models and improve them using feedback from users? We introduce RSI Arena, a two-stage study of autonomous post-training as a step toward recursive self-improvement. Ten frontier models act as training agents, each starting from NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Lightning 30B-A3B Base. During a six-day first stage, each agent has 1,000 GPU-hours and $300 in API credit on a shared 64-GPU cluster, independently selecting data, implementing training procedures, and choosing checkpoints. We evaluate their models on 20 benchmarks and through blind human evaluations. All ten agents produce working assistants, with the strongest model, trained by GPT-6 Astra, closing a median of 76% of the base-to-Instruct gap across 12 capability benchmarks. Its human-preference rating is also close to NVIDIA Instruct after statistical adjustment for answer length and formatting. In Stage 2, each agent receives the comparison records and votes involving its Stage 1 model and is given three additional days for further training. Using NVIDIA Instruct as a common reference across the two evaluation rounds, we observe an improvement from Stage 1 to Stage 2 in the style-adjusted relative rating of eight of the ten models. We show that benchmark gains were modest, with no clear link to preference gains, while some agents encouraged longer responses and one model showed increased harmful compliance on StrongREJECT. RSI Arena provides an auditable setting for studying how human feedback can guide autonomous model development. It takes a step toward recursive self-improvement with human feedback (RSIHF), in which people help define what improvement means for the AI systems they use.

title: ProbeID: Verifying MCP Tool Identity for LLM Agents under Registry Drift
abstract: Agents select tools by copyable descriptions, which cannot establish which implementation runs. ProbeID compares canonicalized responses to schema-valid probes with a trusted admission reference and abstains on ambiguity, so a squatter must copy probe-observable behavior. With the gold present, independent probes and a fixed margin, standard concentration arguments give a shared probe budget logarithmic in the candidate count and bound the joint probability of a wrong decision. On cached MCP-IdentityDrift cases, strict choice reaches \(0.956\) hit@1 while description routers fall near chance, but simpler exact comparisons tie it, MMD better tolerates heavy value noise, and a 32B behavioral judge is similarly accurate at higher cost. Random probes from agent banks and a prospective held-out study of 38 tools test theory-set thresholds. On the agent banks, equality refuses every reachable replacement from 64 probes and the bounded distance from 512, and sharper post hoc gates halve both. Two tools whose drift no bank probe reaches always pass. In an MCP-Bench agent, verification cuts tainted tasks from 15 to 9 of 16 at unchanged task success. Over eleven weeks, 7 of 59 real tools changed responses despite version pins. Verification depends on reference integrity, probe coverage, and response noise.

title: Build or Adopt? Custom-Built vs. General-Purpose LLM Agent Harnesses for Automotive GUI Testing
abstract: As general-purpose LLM agent harnesses mature, organizations must decide whether to continue developing in-house systems or adopt existing alternatives. We study this decision at Volvo Group for GUI testing of Android-based in-vehicle infotainment (IVI) systems. We compare a production, custom-built harness with two general-purpose harnesses, Claude Code and OpenCode, keeping the tools, accessed through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), and the models the same. We evaluate the harnesses with up to four models on Volvo's IVI test cases and on open-ended tasks in public apps (Google Maps, Booking.com), and interview ten practitioners: developers, the product owner, and testers. On Volvo's stepwise IVI tests, general-purpose harnesses match the custom-built harness in success but vary more across runs. Their inference cost per task is 2.6-10.7 times higher, yet the engineering effort they save outweighs this: for a nightly IVI regression suite, total monthly cost, including engineering effort and inference, is 3-66% lower. On open-ended public-app tasks, they succeed more often, mainly because they recover better from incorrect actions. Interviews suggest that external advances can turn an in-house harness into technical debt even without deterioration. Adopting a general-purpose harness shifts maintenance from the agent loop to tools and instructions, but gives teams less control over what the model receives. Regardless of the harness, testers want to inspect the agent's actions and ensure that it follows the prescribed test scenario.

title: AlphaIdeaBench: Benchmarking Automated Research Idea Generation under Feasibility Constraints with Peer Review Alignment
abstract: Research ideas are always proposed under resource constraints: a plan must fit the available compute, API credit, and time. Yet evaluations of research-ideation agents mostly score unconstrained novelty or overlap with a published paper, and their LLM judges are rarely checked against peer review. We introduce AlphaIdeaBench, a benchmark of 100 ideation tasks (50 workshop calls for papers and 50 open problems stated in surveys), each paired with an explicit resource budget and a shared proposal schema. An LLM judge scores each proposal on 12 dimensions covering validity, novelty, and feasibility. To validate the judge, we compare its scores on four novelty axes (problem, method, scenario, and insight) with scores derived from reviewer comments on 600 papers from ICLR 2026, NeurIPS 2025, and ICML 2025. For problem and method novelty, Gemini 3.7 Flash is within one point of the reviewer-derived score on 94-97% of papers; agreement on scenario novelty is relatively lower. We evaluate eight published harnesses on a shared backbone and, within one harness, eight backbone LLMs. CoI-Agent obtains the highest overall score, narrowly ahead of SciMON, which leads on method and insight novelty. All harnesses score low on scenario novelty and rarely change the problem setting. The backbone largely determines which open problem a proposal targets, whereas the harness determines whether a proposal addresses one problem or combines several. Weaker backbones such as Llama 4 Scout fail to carry out that harness's strategy and score low on budget feasibility. Finally, when only the budget is varied on three topics, a larger budget changes the experimental setting on compute-intensive topics but only adds tests on an inexpensive one. We release the tasks, rubrics, and scores to foster standardized, reproducible benchmarking of future research-ideation agents under constraints.

title: Jointly Modeling Preferences and Imperfect Decision-Making in Large Language Models
abstract: Do preferences Large Language Models (LLMs) express in standard elicitation tasks predict their strategic behaviour? LLM agents interacting with humans and other AI systems face potentially conflicting objectives, such as individual welfare, group welfare, and environmental concerns. Prior work characterizes LLM preferences through behavioral-economic and psychological elicitation or strategic games, but rarely tests consistency across settings and prediction in other strategic environments. This requires modeling how competing objectives jointly shape behavior, whereas existing approaches typically measure preference dimensions in isolation. Drawing on utility theory, we introduce the Preference-Behavior Model (PBM), which combines a preference representation with mechanisms capturing imperfect utility maximization. We formulate estimation as an inverse-game problem, jointly inferring preferences and behavioral parameters from observed choices. We evaluate PBM in three social dilemmas that expose conflicting motives: a Public Goods Game, a Collective-Risk Dilemma, and a Common-Pool Resource dilemma. We find that while preferences estimated from established behavioral economic elicitation instruments do not consistently predict behavior in these dilemmas, models fitted in one dilemma retain predictive value in others, suggesting that inferred preferences capture meaningful aspects of LLM decision-making that elicitation instruments may miss. Finally, we assess alignment with persona instructions, finding that inferred preferences broadly reflect intended priorities with specific divergences across dimensions, LLMs, and games being identified by our approach. Our methodology provides a framework for studying how consistently LLM preferences explain behavior, assessing alignment with intended priorities, and revealing trade-offs and behavioral patterns that standard elicitation may miss.

title: Strategic Calibration in LLM Multi-Agent Systems: Audited Pivot Scoring for Truthful Elicitation
abstract: In large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems, reported confidence increasingly determines the allocation of scarce downstream attention, computation, and decision influence. This makes reporting strategic: an agent may overstate the relevance of its contribution even when its underlying belief is well calibrated. Existing calibration methods largely assume passive reporting and therefore do not address strategic incentives created when confidence determines downstream allocation. We formulate strategic calibration as a reporting-layer incentive problem and propose the Audited Pivot Scoring Mechanism (APSM). APSM offsets platform-controlled allocation benefits, uses inverse-propensity-weighted sparse audits, charges the Clarke pivot externality, and applies a strictly proper score. Under the stated model assumptions, truthful reporting is the unique expected-utility best response. We also characterize approximate execution and the audit-variance trade-off. Calculator-free experiments show that LLM agents inflate confidence under Top-$K$ incentives. With a shared agent-local utility interface, LLM agents reduce distortion under both Compensated Proper Scoring (CPS) and APSM. CPS achieves higher exact allocation match, whereas APSM yields lower Brier loss and numerically fewer cutoff crossings. Experiments further show that APSM enlarges the utility margin against allocation-changing deviations by $1.93\times$ and improves robustness under approximate execution. These results support incentive-aware elicitation as a distinct layer for reliable multi-agent coordination.

title: Ring-0 by Default: Agents as Operating Systems (AaOS)
abstract: LLM agents now read and write files, start processes and subagents, fetch network content, load third-party extensions, and save and resume state, which are the responsibilities of an operating system. They gained these functions within about three years, but not the protections that operating systems built over five decades: whatever the model outputs, whether it follows the user, a tool result, or a downloaded skill, runs with the full authority of the host user, in effect at ring 0. Prior work builds an operating system for agents (OS4A); we argue that a deployed agent already is like an operating system (AaOS) and analyze it as one. Taking the mechanisms of standard OS textbooks as a checklist, we map 116 mechanisms in 19 subsystems to their agent counterparts, from product documentation, source code, and the literature, and label each as isomorphic, degraded (function present, protection dependent on the model), missing, mutated, or novel. Only 11 are isomorphic and 65 are missing, most of them protections: privilege separation, resource quotas, transactions, and tamper-proof audit. Existing defenses confine the whole agent or review its extensions and leave this interior unprotected, and by Anderson's reference-monitor criteria (non-bypassable, tamper-proof, verifiable), rules written in the prompt satisfy none.   We test the map with thirteen experiments on Claude Code, Codex CLI, and Gemini CLI, covering 25 mechanisms whose enforcement documentation cannot settle: 16 match the analysis, 7 gain a more precise description, and 2 change verdict. Checks sit in single tools, so the shell bypasses them; all three CLIs load forged transcript records on resume; and task control, sub-agent permissions, and model-based monitors are weak. We identify five problems for which no OS defense transfers and derive a prioritized list of open problems from the gaps of the map.

title: SkillQR: Agentic Skill Discovery for Reason-Intensive Query Rewriting
abstract: Dense retrievers provide grounded evidence that mitigates hallucinations in outputs from Large Language Models (LLMs). Real-world queries are often verbose, ambiguously framed, or require multi-step reasoning, introducing irrelevant details that weaken semantic matching for dense retrievers. Query rewriting is a widely adopted pre-retrieval technique that leverages LLMs to reformulate queries and bridge the semantic gap between such queries and the retrieval target. Existing rewriting approaches either rely on expensive proprietary models, substantial training data, or iterative retrieval and rewriting, while largely applying a uniform rewriting strategy regardless of the retrieval corpus. We observe that effective query rewriting instructions are not universal: the optimal strategy depends on the retrieval target, rather than the model alone. We introduce SkillQR, a query rewriting framework that automatically discovers reasoning strategy sets from the retrieval target and dynamically routes a query to the appropriate rewriting strategy at inference time. Without relying on training data, SkillQR achieves competitive performance compared to fine-tuned rewriting models on the BRIGHT and R2MED benchmarks, while also providing lower inference latency than iterative rewriting approaches.
